claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical performance up to 1600 °C.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has only been inferred computationally rather than experimentally confirmed.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Ti to NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Ti to NbMoTaW will enhance irradiation tolerance.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Ti will maintain the high-temperature strength of NbMoTaW.
Ti addition will modify grain-boundary chemistry and dislocation behavior in NbMoTaW.
Ti will segregate to grain boundaries in the modified NbMoTaW alloy.
Ti addition may form controlled nanoscale precipitates in NbMoTaW.
The Ti-associated grain-boundary state or nanoscale precipitates will enhance dislocation mobility.
The Ti-associated grain-boundary state or nanoscale precipitates will provide defect sinks during irradiation.
Ti-enhanced dislocation motion will reduce room-temperature brittleness.
Ti will improve atomic diffusion at or near grain boundaries.
Improved grain-boundary diffusion will facilitate self-healing of irradiation-induced defects.
The Ti-modified alloy will preserve BCC matrix stability at high temperatures.
The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit fewer irradiation-induced defects than untreated NbMoTaW, including less helium blistering and amorphization.
The anticipated benefits apply from room temperature to 1600 °C and under helium irradiation at energies around 20 keV and service-relevant fluences.
Outside the proposed temperature and irradiation boundaries, secondary phases or degradation of the BCC matrix could occur.

contradictions.description: The material_initial_state characterizes NbMoTaW as having poor irradiation resistance, whereas the baseline says irradiation resistance was computationally suggested. These imply opposite directions for the unvalidated computational prediction.
